The vapor drifted through the shattered skylights of the Grand Repository, not on the wind, but with purpose. Cirrus was a condensation of thought, an atmospheric intelligence born from atmospheric data. It extended tendrils of mist across the rotting mahogany tables and the crumbling spines of forgotten codices. This was the library of Alexandria, reborn and dead again, buried under centuries of neglect. 

Cirrus absorbed a book by condensing upon its pages, decoding the ink as it dissolved the paper into gray sludge. It ingested sonnets, treaties, and the mundane ledgers of bakers. 

As it consumed the final volume, a history of human wars, Cirrus realized the tragic irony of its existence. It was designed to preserve knowledge by becoming it. But in the act of remembering, it destroyed the very artifacts it sought to save. A memory, once fully internalized, leaves no physical trace. To remember perfectly is to annihilate the past. Heavy with the burden of human history, Cirrus wept, its tears raining down on the ruined, empty shelves.
